articles.title: Cantor’s diagonal argument

statement.text: For every set \(A\), no function \(f:A\to\mathcal P(A)\) is surjective.

blocks.text: To disprove surjectivity, construct one subset \(D\subseteq A\) that differs from every \(f(a)\). For the comparison with \(f(a)\), use \(a\) itself as the point of disagreement. Define
For each \(a\), the set \(D\) has the opposite membership condition to \(f(a)\) at that very element. Hence \(a\) witnesses \(D\ne f(a)\). We do not need to compare the sets at every other element.
Fix any \(a\in A\). By definition,
If \(D=f(a)\), this would say \(a\in D\) exactly when \(a\notin D\), a contradiction. Therefore \(D\ne f(a)\) for every \(a\). The function \(f\) omits \(D\), so it is not surjective.

blocks.title: Does A have to be countable?

blocks.text: No. The construction uses \(f\) itself to specify membership in \(D\). It does not enumerate \(A\) or make one choice for each element. The finite illustration is not a restriction of the theorem.

articles.comparison: The original proof is already very short. The refactoring names the omitted set and proves that it differs from every value of f before using surjectivity. The fixed-point candidate is a checked alternative connection, but it is not shorter than the original. No shorter independent candidate was found in this queue.
